title: Akka Mahadevi
hook: a woman arrives at a hall of saints with nothing but her hair, and the first thing she gets is a hard question

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akka Mahadevi, elder sister, and the silkworm caught in its own threads. Did you catch a wanting at its first turn? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

A gathering of saints in the city of Kalyana. People come there to talk about God plainly, and to be tested. In walks a young woman who has left a king's house. She has given up her clothes on the road. Her long hair is all that covers her. Before she can sit, one of the saints, known for his searching questions, looks at her and asks a question that would make anyone flinch. Her answer is what the story keeps. Today, the walk from the palace, and the test at the door.
screen: `A GATHERING OF SAINTS.` → `ONLY HER HAIR.` → `A QUESTION AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, as her tradition tells it, in paraphrase. A local king, Kaushika, wants Mahadevi. The tellings differ on what happens next: some say she refuses him, some that she marries him on conditions he goes on to break. Either way, she leaves. Her vachanas speak of it plainly. Her husband, she says, is the lord white as jasmine, and she has no use for one who dies and decays. She walks away from the palace, sheds her clothes, and goes on, covered by her hair. On the road, she comes to Kalyana, where the Virashaiva saints gather around Basavanna in a hall the tradition calls the Anubhava Mantapa, the hall of experience. There Allama Prabhu, a teacher famous in the stories for his hard questions, tests her. He asks, roughly: if you've truly given up the body's shame, why hide behind your hair? It's a fair question, and a cruel one, and she doesn't dodge it. Her answer comes in more than one form. In one, she says that until the fruit is ripe, the skin doesn't fall away. In another, that the covering is for the people looking, so the sight of her won't trouble them. Both answers refuse to pretend. She doesn't claim to be finished. She says she's ripening. And she thinks about the people around her, not only her own freedom. And the saints don't send her away. Tradition says they welcome her, and call her Akka, elder sister. The test was the door, and she walked through it.
screen: `SHE LEAVES THE KING'S HOUSE` · `THE HALL OF EXPERIENCE` · `ALLAMA'S HARD QUESTION` · `UNTIL THE FRUIT IS RIPE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: still ripening. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one place in your life where you're not finished yet. A habit, a hurt, a hope. Don't scold it, and don't pretend it's done. Just say to yourself, quietly: still ripening. Breathe in, and let it be unfinished. Breathe out, and let it grow in its own time. If you pray, you can offer the unripe part to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Akka Mahadevi. She left a king for the lord white as jasmine, came to Kalyana in only her hair, and answered Allama's test: until the fruit is ripe, the skin stays on. Today's word.
Your line: Akka Mahadevi. Today, when someone asks a hard question, try answering honestly about what's still unfinished. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Lingayat tradition tells Akka Mahadevi's arrival at Kalyana and her exchange with Allama Prabhu in its collections of the saints' dialogues, and her story is staged, sung and taught in Karnataka.
